chapters.n: After Ahab’s death, Moab—a kingdom east of the Dead Sea that Omri had conquered—breaks free. The Moabite Stone, an inscription by King Mesha, tells this same story from Moab’s side.
King Ahaziah falls through a latticed window or railing on his upper floor and is badly hurt. Instead of turning to the Lord, he sends to the Philistine god of Ekron to ask whether he will recover.

f.g: a wooden grille on a window or rooftop railing.
‘lord of flies,’ probably a mocking alteration of Baal-zebul, ‘Baal the prince.’
one of the five main Philistine cities.

chapters.n: The Lord sends Elijah to intercept the messengers with a pointed question: Is there no God in Israel, that you go to a foreign idol?

f.g: the Lord’s heavenly messenger.

chapters.n: The answer to the king’s question comes from the true God, not Baal-zebub: he will never leave his bed.
The messengers return early, and the king asks why.
They repeat the stranger’s words exactly.
The king asks what the man looked like.

f.g: what kind of man; what did he look like?

chapters.n: Their description—a hairy man (or a man in a hairy cloak) with a leather belt—is instantly recognizable. John the Baptist, who came “in the spirit and power of Elias,” dressed the same way.

f.g: possibly ‘a man wearing a garment of hair.’

f.w: girt with a girdle of leather

f.g: an officer commanding a unit of fifty soldiers.

chapters.n: Elijah answers with wordplay: if he truly is a “man of God,” let fire come down. Fire falls and consumes the captain and his men—showing who really holds power.

f.w: let fire come down from heaven

chapters.n: A second captain comes with fifty more and is even more demanding: “Come down quickly!”
Fire falls again and consumes them.
The third captain kneels and humbly pleads for his life and the lives of his men. Humility changes the outcome.

f.g: begged, pleaded with.

chapters.n: He acknowledges what happened to the others and asks for mercy.
The angel tells Elijah it is safe to go. Elijah comes down willingly to deliver God’s message in person.
Elijah repeats the sentence face to face: because the king sought Baal-zebub, he will die.

f.g: ‘Jehovah is exalted’; also spelled Joram. Two kings with this name ruled at the same time in Israel and Judah.

chapters.n: Ahaziah’s reign was brief and is recorded in Israel’s royal annals.

f.g: probably a town in the hills near Bethel, not the Gilgal by the Jordan.

chapters.n: Three times Elijah urges Elisha to stay behind, and three times Elisha refuses with a solemn oath. His loyalty is being tested—and proven.

f.g: stay, wait.

chapters.n: The prophetic community at Bethel knows Elijah will be taken today. Elisha knows too, and asks them to keep quiet—he doesn’t want to talk about it.

f.g: members of a prophetic fellowship or school.
from being your leader and master.
be quiet.

chapters.n: The second test: Elijah heads to Jericho, and Elisha again refuses to leave him.
The prophets at Jericho also know, and Elisha gives the same reply.
The third test: Elijah goes to the Jordan, and Elisha stays at his side.
Fifty prophets watch from a distance as the two stand by the river.
Elijah rolls up his cloak and strikes the water, which parts so they cross on dry ground—echoing Moses at the Red Sea and Joshua at this very river.

f.g: a prophet’s outer cloak.

chapters.n: Elijah invites a final request. Elisha asks for a “double portion” of his spirit—the inheritance share of a firstborn son. He is asking to be Elijah’s true successor.

f.g: the firstborn son’s inheritance, twice the share of other sons.

chapters.n: Elijah says it is a hard request, beyond his power to grant. If Elisha is permitted to see him taken, that will be the sign the Lord has granted it.

f.g: separated the two of them.

f.g: tore them, a sign of mourning.

chapters.n: They pester him until he is embarrassed to keep refusing, so he lets them go. A three-day search finds nothing.

causing miscarriage or unfruitfulness.

chapters.n: Elisha asks for a new bowl filled with salt. A new vessel suggests something clean and set apart.

Near Bethel, the center of calf worship, a gang of young men mocks Elisha: “Go up, baldhead!”—possibly sneering at Elijah’s ascension and insulting God’s prophet.

chapters.n: Elisha curses them in the Lord’s name, and two bears maul forty-two of them. The story warns how seriously God regards contempt for His word and servants in that apostate city.

chapters.n: Elisha travels to Mount Carmel, scene of Elijah’s great victory, and then to the capital, Samaria.

f.g: a standing stone or sacred pillar dedicated to Baal.

chapters.n: He held on to Jeroboam’s golden-calf worship, which every northern king kept as state policy.

chapters.n: Mesha of Moab was a breeder of sheep and paid Israel a huge annual tribute in lambs and wool. Mesha’s own inscription, the Moabite Stone (about 840 BC), names him and describes Israel’s domination.

sheep breeder.

Jehoram musters Israel’s army to bring Moab back under control.

The three kings—Israel, Judah, and Edom—march seven days by a roundabout route and run out of water for the army and animals.

chapters.n: Jehoram despairs, blaming the Lord for bringing them out to die—oddly invoking the Lord he does not serve.

respect, honor.

f.g: a small, easy matter.

chapters.n: At the time of the morning offering at the temple, water flows in from Edom—perhaps from a distant storm—and fills the land.

f.g: the grain offering made each morning.

chapters.n: Moab mobilizes every man old enough to bear arms and takes position on the border.

They assume the three allied kings have turned on each other and rush to loot the camp.

f.g: go and plunder!

soldiers who hurled stones with slings.

f.w: offered him for a burnt offering

chapters.n: He tells her to borrow as many empty jars as she can from her neighbors—“not a few.” The size of her blessing will match the size of her faith.

f.g: from outside, around the neighborhood.

chapters.n: She is to shut the door and pour oil into every jar. The miracle happens privately, within the family.
She obeys, and her sons keep bringing jars as she pours.
When the last jar is full, the oil stops. The supply lasted exactly as long as there were vessels to receive it.

f.g: stopped, ceased flowing.

chapters.n: Elisha tells her to sell the oil, pay the debt, and live on the rest. The Lord provided not just rescue but a future.
In Shunem, a wealthy and influential woman insists that Elisha eat at her home, and he makes it a regular stop.

f.g: a village in the Jezreel Valley, on the route between Carmel and Samaria.
a woman of wealth and standing.
urged, insisted.

chapters.n: She recognizes Elisha as a holy man of God and proposes to her husband that they do more for him.
They build a small rooftop room furnished with a bed, table, chair, and lamp—a thoughtful act of hospitality to God’s servant.

f.g: a small upper room built on the roof.
a lampstand.

chapters.n: On one visit Elisha rests in the room.
He sends his servant Gehazi to call the woman.

chapters.n: Through Gehazi, Elisha offers to speak to the king or army commander on her behalf. She politely declines—she is content and secure among her own people.

f.g: you have gone to so much trouble for us.

Elisha calls her, and she stands respectfully in the doorway.
He promises that by this time next year she will hold a son. She begs him not to raise false hopes—her longing runs deep.

f.w: according to the time of life
f.g: when the season comes round again; about a year from now.

chapters.n: The promise is fulfilled; she bears a son at the time Elisha said.
Years later, the boy goes out to his father in the harvest fields.

f.g: harvest workers.

chapters.n: He cries, “My head, my head!”—perhaps sunstroke. His father has a servant carry him home.

f.g: a young servant.

chapters.n: The boy sits on his mother’s lap until noon, then dies.
Without a word to anyone, she lays him on the prophet’s bed and shuts the door—an act of quiet faith that the man of God is the key.
She asks her husband for a servant and a donkey so she can hurry to Elisha.

f.g: donkeys.

chapters.n: Her husband, unaware of the death, wonders why she would go on an ordinary day. She simply says, “It will be well.”

f.g: holy days when people might visit a prophet.
Hebrew shalom: ‘peace,’ ‘all is well.’

chapters.n: She tells the servant to drive hard and not slow down for her sake.

f.g: don’t slow down.

chapters.n: She rides about twenty-five miles to Mount Carmel. Elisha sees her coming in the distance.

f.g: over there.

chapters.n: Elisha sends Gehazi to ask whether all is well. She answers, “It is well,” saving her grief for the prophet himself.

She falls and grasps Elisha’s feet in anguish. Gehazi tries to push her away, but Elisha stops him: she is in bitter distress, and the Lord has not revealed why. Prophets do not know everything unless God reveals it.

f.g: bitter, deeply distressed.

Elisha sends Gehazi ahead with his staff, instructing him not to stop for greetings. Ancient greetings could be long and elaborate.

don’t stop to greet anyone.

chapters.n: The mother refuses to leave without Elisha himself, using the same oath Elisha once spoke to Elijah. Elisha goes with her.
Gehazi lays the staff on the boy, but nothing happens. The child does not wake.
Elisha arrives to find the boy dead on his own bed.
He shuts the door and prays to the Lord. The power is God’s, not the prophet’s.

f.g: two.

chapters.n: Elisha stretches himself over the child, mouth to mouth, eye to eye, hand to hand—just as Elijah once did—and the boy’s body grows warm.

f.g: grew, became.

chapters.n: After pacing and stretching himself out again, the boy sneezes seven times and opens his eyes. Seven suggests completeness: he is fully restored.
Elisha has Gehazi call the mother and tells her, “Take up your son.”
She falls at his feet in gratitude, then takes her son. Hebrews remembers such women: “Women received their dead raised to life again.”
During a famine at Gilgal, Elisha has a large pot of stew cooked for the prophets studying with him.

f.g: famine, scarcity.
boil a stew.
gathered as disciples receiving instruction.

chapters.n: Someone gathers wild gourds from an unknown vine and slices them into the stew. Many think these were bitter, poisonous colocynth gourds.

f.g: probably colocynth, a bitter, poisonous gourd.

chapters.n: Tasting it, the men cry out, “There is death in the pot!”

f.g: flour.

chapters.n: A man brings Elisha firstfruits—twenty barley loaves and fresh grain. Firstfruits were normally given to priests; here they go to God’s prophet.

f.g: grain, not American maize.

chapters.n: Elisha’s servant protests that twenty loaves can’t feed a hundred men. Elisha says the Lord promises they will eat and have leftovers.

f.g: servant, attendant.

chapters.n: They eat and food is left over. This miracle foreshadows Jesus feeding the multitudes with barley loaves.

Naaman is Aram’s top general—respected, victorious, and brave. Surprisingly, the text credits his victories to the Lord, the God of Israel, who rules all nations. Yet he has a skin disease that no rank can cure.

chapters.n: Aramean raiders had captured a young Israelite girl, who now serves Naaman’s wife. She has lost home and family.

f.g: in raiding bands.
a young girl.

chapters.n: Rather than bitterness, the girl shows compassion and faith: she wishes her master could meet the prophet in Samaria, who could heal him. One small, faithful voice starts the whole story.

f.g: ‘If only…’; ‘I wish…’
cure him.

chapters.n: Naaman reports her words to the king of Aram.
The king sends Naaman with a letter and a fortune in gifts—about 750 pounds of silver, 150 pounds of gold, and ten sets of fine clothing. He assumes healing can be bought.

f.g: ‘Go on, go.’
sets of fine clothes.

chapters.n: The letter asks Israel’s king to cure Naaman, as though the king controlled the prophet.
Israel’s king (probably Jehoram) panics and tears his robes: only God can give life or death. He assumes Aram is looking for an excuse for war. He does not even think of Elisha.

chapters.n: Elisha sends word: “Send him to me, and he will know there is a prophet in Israel.”
Naaman arrives in grand style with horses and chariots and waits at Elisha’s door.

chapters.n: Naaman is furious. He expected a dramatic ceremony with the prophet waving his hand over the diseased spot.

chapters.n: Naaman returns to confess: there is no God in all the earth except in Israel. He offers Elisha a gift.

f.g: a gift, a present.

Naaman asks for two mule-loads of Israel’s soil to take home, so he can worship the Lord on Israelite earth. He vows to worship no other god.

f.g: many ancients believed a god was tied to his land; Naaman wanted to worship on Israel’s soil.

chapters.n: He asks pardon in advance: his duty will require him to support his king as he bows in the temple of Rimmon, Aram’s storm god. His conscience is now sensitive.

Naaman was the king’s attendant officer.

chapters.n: Elisha simply says, “Go in peace,” leaving the matter between Naaman and God.

chapters.n: Gehazi thinks his master was foolish to let this rich foreigner go without paying. He swears he will get something—greed taking the Lord’s name in vain.

Naaman generously gives double and has servants carry it.

stored, hid.

chapters.n: The prophetic community under Elisha is growing, and their meeting place has become too small.

chapters.n: By midsummer the food runs out completely. Lamentations describes the horror of famine during this siege.
When the Babylonians break through the wall, Zedekiah and his soldiers flee at night through a gate near the royal garden, heading east toward the Jordan Valley.

f.g: The wall was breached.
Hebrew Arabah—the Jordan Valley, toward Jericho.

chapters.n: The Babylonians catch Zedekiah near Jericho, and his army deserts him.
Zedekiah is brought to Nebuchadnezzar’s field headquarters at Riblah in Syria for sentencing as a rebel vassal who had broken his oath.

Zedekiah’s sons are killed before his eyes—the last thing he ever sees—and then he is blinded and taken to Babylon. The Book of Mormon reveals that one son, Mulek, escaped and was led to the Americas.

f.g: Ezekiel had foretold Zedekiah would be brought to Babylon yet not see it (Ezekiel 12:13).
Bronze chains or shackles.

chapters.n: About a month later, Nebuzaradan, commander of Nebuchadnezzar’s guard, arrives to finish the job.

f.g: Literally “chief of the butchers” or executioners—commander of the royal bodyguard.

f.w: the fifth month, on the seventh day

chapters.n: He burns Solomon’s temple, the palace and every important house. The temple had stood for nearly four centuries; Jews still mourn its loss each year on the ninth of Av.

f.w: burnt the house of the LORD

chapters.n: The army tears down Jerusalem’s walls, leaving the city defenseless. Nehemiah would rebuild them about 140 years later.
The rest of the population, including those who had defected to Babylon, is deported.

f.w: fell away to the king of Babylon
f.g: Deserted to Babylon’s side, as Jeremiah had urged (Jeremiah 38:2).

chapters.n: Only the poorest are left to tend vineyards and fields, so the land would not become completely wild.

f.g: Vineyard workers and farmers.

f.w: left of the poor of the land

chapters.n: The great bronze pillars, stands and the huge bronze basin Solomon made are smashed so the metal can be hauled to Babylon.

f.g: A huge bronze basin of water for priestly washing, resting on twelve bronze oxen.

chapters.n: All the smaller bronze utensils used in temple sacrifices are taken as well.

f.g: Tools for trimming lamp wicks.

chapters.n: Anything made of gold or silver is carried off too. Some of these vessels later appear in Belshazzar’s feast and were returned under Cyrus.

f.g: Pans for carrying hot coals from the altar.

f.w: such things as were of gold

chapters.n: The bronze of Solomon’s pillars, sea and stands was so great it could not be weighed—a poignant reminder of past glory now lost.

f.g: Too much to weigh.

chapters.n: The narrator pauses to describe one pillar: about 27 feet tall with a 4½-foot bronze capital decorated with chainwork and pomegranates. Lingering on the detail expresses grief over what was destroyed.

f.g: A cubit is about 18 inches (45 cm), the length from elbow to fingertip.
The capital, or decorative top, of a pillar.

chapters.n: Nebuzaradan arrests the chief priests and temple gatekeepers. Seraiah the chief priest was an ancestor of Ezra the scribe.
He also takes military officers, royal advisers, the scribe in charge of the draft, and sixty prominent men—those seen as leaders of the rebellion.

f.g: Sixty (a score is twenty).
Enrolled or called up for military service.

chapters.n: These leaders are brought to Nebuchadnezzar at Riblah.

f.w: brought them to the king of Babylon

chapters.n: They are executed, and the narrator sums up the tragedy in one line: Judah was exiled from its land. The covenant warnings of Deuteronomy have come true.

f.w: So Judah was carried away out of their land

chapters.n: Nebuchadnezzar appoints Gedaliah as governor over those left behind. Gedaliah came from Shaphan’s family, which had supported Josiah’s reforms and protected Jeremiah.

f.w: Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, the son of Shaphan

chapters.n: Surviving Judean army captains and their men gather to Gedaliah at Mizpah, his new capital north of Jerusalem.

f.g: A town a few miles north of Jerusalem, in Benjamin.

chapters.n: Gedaliah urges them to accept Babylon’s rule and settle down peacefully—the same counsel Jeremiah had given.

f.w: serve the king of Babylon; and it shall be well with you

chapters.n: A few months later Ishmael, a member of the royal family, murders Gedaliah and those with him—destroying the last hope of stable life in Judah.

f.g: Of the royal family; Ishmael may have resented a non-royal governor.

chapters.n: Fearing Babylonian revenge, the remaining people flee to Egypt—ironically returning to the land of bondage. They forced Jeremiah to go with them.
The book closes with a glimmer of hope. In 561 BC, after 37 years in captivity, Jehoiachin is released from prison by Babylon’s new king.

f.g: Amel-Marduk, son of Nebuchadnezzar; the name means “man of Marduk,” not “evil.”
An idiom for showing favor or releasing someone (compare Genesis 40:13).

chapters.n: The Babylonian king treats Jehoiachin kindly and honors him above other captive kings.

f.w: set his throne above the throne of the kings

chapters.n: Jehoiachin trades prison clothes for royal ones and eats regularly at the king’s table. Babylonian ration tablets even mention food given to “Jehoiachin, king of Judah.”

f.g: A symbol of restored dignity.

chapters.n: He receives a daily allowance for life. Ending here, the book quietly signals that David’s line survives and God’s promises are not finished; Jehoiachin’s descendants include Zerubbabel and, in Matthew’s genealogy, Jesus.

f.w: all the days of his life
